supporting_arguments.exact_current_paragraph:
1.1 For $k\ne0$, apply [F1] to $u=k_j/2$ in each coordinate and square the bounds. Summing yields
$$\frac{4}{\pi^2}|k|_2^2\le D_d(k)\le |k|_2^2,$$
where $|k|_2^2=\sum_jk_j^2$. The denominator is positive off the origin, so its reciprocal is continuous on the cube with the origin removed. Extending it by the stated value at the closed singleton $\{0\}$ makes it Borel measurable: each open-set preimage is the union of a Borel subset of that complement and, when applicable, the singleton. The cosine numerator is continuous, so all nonnegative comparison integrands below are measurable by [F4]. [given, F1, F4, algebra]

2.1 For $j\ge0$, let $Q_j=[-2^{-j},2^{-j}]^d\setminus[-2^{-(j+1)},2^{-(j+1)}]^d$. The sets are pairwise disjoint, are contained in $[-1,1]^d$, and by [F2] have measure $(2^d-1)2^{-jd}$. On $Q_j$, $|k|_2\ge\|k\|_\infty>2^{-(j+1)}$, so step 1.1 gives $(\kappa D_d(k))^{-1}\le (\pi^2/(4\kappa))2^{2j+2}$. Hence
$$\int_{Q_j}(\kappa D_d(k))^{-1}\,d\lambda_d(k)\le \frac{\pi^2}{\kappa}(2^d-1)2^{(2-d)j}.$$
For $d>2$, these upper bounds sum to a finite geometric series by [F4]. On the remaining part of $[-\pi,\pi]^d$ outside $[-1,1]^d$, $|k|_2\ge1$, so step 1.1 bounds $(\kappa D_d)^{-1}$ by $\pi^2/(4\kappa)$; that part has finite measure by [F2]. Countable additivity and monotone convergence in [F3] therefore show that $(\kappa D_d)^{-1}$ is integrable on the whole cube. [given, F2, F3, F4, step 1.1, algebra]

2.2 For $1\le d\le2$, step 1.1 gives $(\kappa D_d(k))^{-1}\ge(\kappa|k|_2^2)^{-1}$ on every $Q_j$. There $|k|_2\le\sqrt d\,2^{-j}$, and hence
$$\int_{Q_j}(\kappa D_d(k))^{-1}\,d\lambda_d(k)\ge \frac{1}{\kappa d}(2^d-1)2^{(2-d)j}.$$
The right side is bounded below by the positive constant $(2^d-1)/(\kappa d)$ for all $j\ge0$ when $d\le2$. Since the $Q_j$ are disjoint, finite additivity in [F3] shows that the integral over their first $M+1$ layers is at least $(M+1)(2^d-1)/(\kappa d)$; letting $M\to\infty$ and using monotonicity gives $\int(\kappa D_d)^{-1}=+\infty$. [given, F3, step 1.1, algebra]

$$\partial_{x_j}\varphi_b(x)=b^{-(d-2)/2}b^{-1}(\partial_{x'_j}\varphi')(x/b)=b^{-d/2}(\partial_{x'_j}\varphi')(x/b).$$
Thus $|\nabla\varphi_b(x)|^2=b^{-d}|\nabla\varphi'(x/b)|^2$. Applying [F1] with $T$ to this nonnegative integrand gives
$$S_2[\varphi_b]=\frac12\int_{\mathbb R^d}b^{-d}|\nabla\varphi'(x')|^2b^d\,d\lambda_d(x')=S_2[\varphi'].$$
The compact support and smoothness assumptions make these integrands measurable and finite. [given, F1, F2, algebra]

2.1 The same change of variables gives
$$Q_4[\varphi_b]=\frac1{4!}\int_{\mathbb R^d}b^{-2(d-2)}\varphi'(x/b)^4\,d\lambda_d(x) =b^{d-2(d-2)}Q_4[\varphi']=b^{4-d}Q_4[\varphi'].$$
Therefore $gQ_4[\varphi_b]=g'Q_4[\varphi']$ with $g'=b^{4-d}g$, as claimed. [given, F1, algebra] ∎

supporting_arguments.exact_current_paragraph: 2.1 Choose independent generators $S_1,\ldots,S_r$ from those commuting involutions and set $\Pi=2^{-r}\prod_{j=1}^r(I+S_j)$. This is an orthogonal projection. Independence of the vertex and face support vectors implies that its $2^r$ Pauli terms are distinct and only the all-identity term is the identity matrix. Every other Pauli term has trace zero because at least one tensor factor is $X$, $Z$, or $XZ$, each of which has trace zero. Thus $\operatorname{Tr}\Pi=2^{-r}2^{|E|}>0$, so the common $+1$ eigenspace is nonzero and has dimension $2^{|E|-r}$. Each penalty is an orthogonal projection by step 1.1, and for every $\psi$ the quadratic form is $\langle\psi,H_K\psi\rangle=\sum_{v\in V}J_v\left\|\frac{I-A_v}{2}\psi\right\|^2+\sum_{f\in F}K_f\left\|\frac{I-B_f}{2}\psi\right\|^2$. Positivity of every coupling makes this quantity zero exactly when every penalty annihilates $\psi$, equivalently when every stabilizer has eigenvalue $+1$. Thus $\ker H_K$ is the common $+1$ eigenspace, the Hamiltonian is frustration free, and its ground space has dimension $2^{|E|-r}$. [F1, step 1.1, step 1.3, algebra]

2.2 Put $m=\min(\{J_v\}\cup\{K_f\})$. The commuting self-adjoint penalty projections have a common orthonormal eigenbasis: diagonalize one projection and restrict the remaining commuting projections to each invariant eigenspace, iterating over the finite family. Thus every eigenvalue of $H_K$ occurs on a joint eigenvector. Outside the ground space, such a vector violates at least one constraint; by the two product identities of step 1.2, at least two constraints of that same type are violated. Each contributes at least $m$, so every excited eigenvalue is at least $2m$ above the ground energy zero. If the orthogonal complement of the ground space is zero, the stated $+\infty$ convention applies. [given, step 1.2, algebra]

supporting_arguments.exact_current_paragraph: 1.1 The operators $A_v,B_f$ are commuting self-adjoint involutions by [F1], so $\Pi=\prod_{v\in V}(I+A_v)/2\prod_{f\in F}(I+B_f)/2$ is the orthogonal projection onto their common $+1$ eigenspace. Expand this finite product. Each term is a tensor-product Pauli $X(a)Z(b)$ with coefficient $+1$: factors of the same type multiply without phases, and every vertex operator commutes with every face operator. For the ordinary matrix trace on $\mathcal H_K$, the trace of a tensor product is the product of the factor traces. A nonidentity Pauli therefore has trace zero because at least one edge factor is $X$, $Z$, or $XZ$, each of which has trace zero; an identity term has trace $2^{|E|}$. The empty subset contributes one identity term and no term contributes negative trace, so $\operatorname{Tr}\Pi\ge 2^{|E|-|V|-|F|}>0$. Thus $\Pi\ne0$. Since each penalty is an orthogonal projection and the couplings are positive, for every $\psi$ the quadratic form is $\langle\psi,H_K\psi\rangle=\sum_{v\in V}J_v\left\|\frac{I-A_v}{2}\psi\right\|^2+\sum_{f\in F}K_f\left\|\frac{I-B_f}{2}\psi\right\|^2$. This is zero exactly when every penalty annihilates $\psi$, equivalently when every stabilizer has eigenvalue $+1$. Hence $\ker H_K$ is the common $+1$ eigenspace and is nonzero, so it contains a ground vector of energy zero. [given, F1, algebra]

2.1 Let $b\in\mathbb F_2^E$ be the edge chain of the primal path $\gamma$. Because the path visits no vertex twice and has distinct endpoints, each internal vertex has even path incidence and the endpoints have odd incidence, so $\partial_1b=v_1+v_2$. For each vertex $v$, $Z(b)A_v=(-1)^{\langle b,\partial_1^Tv\rangle}A_vZ(b)=(-1)^{(\partial_1b)_v}A_vZ(b)$; $Z(b)$ commutes with every $B_f$. Hence applying $Z(b)$ to any ground vector flips exactly $A_{v_1}$ and $A_{v_2}$ from $+1$ to $-1$ and leaves every other stabilizer eigenvalue unchanged. [given, F1, step 1.1, algebra]

2.2 Regard the dual path $\gamma^*$ as a path in the dual graph whose vertices are faces, and let $a\in\mathbb F_2^E$ indicate the primal edges crossed by its dual edges. By the definition of the dual incidence map as $\partial_2^T$, the no-repeated-face hypothesis and distinct endpoint faces give $\partial_2^Ta=f_1+f_2$. For each face $f$, $X(a)B_f=(-1)^{\langle a,\partial_2f\rangle}B_fX(a)=(-1)^{(\partial_2^Ta)_f}B_fX(a)$; $X(a)$ commutes with every $A_v$. Hence applying $X(a)$ to any ground vector flips exactly $B_{f_1}$ and $B_{f_2}$ and leaves every other stabilizer eigenvalue unchanged. [given, F1, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 By step 2.1, the vector $Z(b)\psi$ has eigenvalue $-1$ precisely for the two vertex stabilizers at $v_1,v_2$ and eigenvalue $+1$ for every other stabilizer, when $\psi$ is a ground vector. Thus the only nonzero terms in $H_K Z(b)\psi$ are the penalties $J_{v_i}(I-A_{v_i})/2$, each acting as multiplication by $J_{v_i}$; its $H_K$-eigenvalue, and hence its energy increase from the ground eigenvalue zero, is $J_{v_1}+J_{v_2}$. [F1, step 2.1, algebra]

supporting_arguments.exact_current_paragraph: 2.1 For each compact $J=[-A,A]\subset\mathbb R$, $f(x,t):=e^{-\beta x^2}\cosh(tx)$ and $\partial_t f=x e^{-\beta x^2}\sinh(tx)$ are continuous on $(0,\infty)\times\mathbb R$. The inequality $A x\le \beta x^2/2+A^2/(2\beta)$ bounds $|\partial_t f|$ on $J$ by $e^{A^2/(2\beta)}x e^{-\beta x^2/2}$, whose integral is $e^{A^2/(2\beta)}/\beta<\infty$; the base slice $f(x,0)=e^{-\beta x^2}$ is absolutely integrable by [F1] and [F3] with the increasing $C^1$ bijection $u=\sqrt\beta x:(0,\infty)\to(0,\infty)$, whose derivative is the positive constant $\sqrt\beta$. Thus [F2] applies and $F'(a)=\int_0^\infty x e^{-\beta x^2}\sinh(ax)\,dx$. Differentiating the closed form in step 1.1 yields $F'(a)=a\sqrt\pi\,e^{a^2/(4\beta)}/(4\beta^{3/2})$. [given, F1, F2, F3, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 Let $h(E):=\rho_0(E)e^{-\beta E}$ and $\phi(x):=x^2$ on $(0,\infty)$. The map $\phi$ is an increasing $C^1$ bijection with $\phi'(x)=2x>0$; on each compact truncation its proper change-of-variable hypotheses hold, and $h$ is locally continuous. By [A1], the transformed integrand is $2x h(x^2)=e^{S_0}C\pi^{-2}x e^{-\beta x^2}\sinh(ax)$, whose improper integral is finite by step 2.1. Thus [F3] gives $Z_0(\beta)=\int_0^\infty h(E)\,dE=\int_0^\infty h(x^2)2x\,dx=e^{S_0}C\pi^{-2}F'(a)$, where $a=2\pi\sqrt{2C}$. Substitution of step 2.1 gives the stated formula for $Z_0$. It is finite and strictly positive because $C,\beta>0$ and the displayed factors are finite and positive. [given, A1, F3, step 2.1, algebra]

4.1 For $f(E,\beta):=\rho_0(E)e^{-\beta E}$ on $(0,\infty)\times(0,\infty)$, both $f$ and $\partial_\beta f=-E\rho_0(E)e^{-\beta E}$ are continuous. On a compact $J\subset(0,\infty)$ let $\beta_0:=\min J>0$. Since $\sinh(a\sqrt E)\le e^{a\sqrt E}/2$ and $a\sqrt E\le \beta_0 E/2+a^2/(2\beta_0)$, the derivative magnitude is bounded on $J$ by a constant times $E e^{-\beta_0 E/2}$, which has finite integral; the same estimate without the factor $E$ gives an integrable base slice. Apply [F2] on $(0,\infty)$ to differentiate $Z_0$: $Z_0'(\beta)=-\int_0^\infty E\rho_0(E)e^{-\beta E}\,dE$. Hence $\bar E=-\partial_\beta\log Z_0=3/(2\beta)+2\pi^2C/\beta^2$. [given, A1, F2, step 3.1, algebra]
